10568-dual-control-ship-s-company-part-8:
In another tale from W. W. Jacobs's Ship's Company, a young man named Albert Sharp hopes to win Florrie, while her father offers kind but useless advice. Mr. Culpepper likes Sharp and calls him steady, yet warns that girls do not always favor steady young men. The older man's own marriage supplies the joke, since he and his wife now want different things.

The comedy turns on courtship, family meddling, and the clash between what parents say and what young people feel. Sharp can argue well at his debating club but falters when he must speak to Florrie herself. Readers get a light, funny story about love, pride, and the small wars fought inside a household.
10788-peter-s-pence-sailor-s-knots-part-:
W. W. Jacobs's "Peter's Pence," the eighth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, starts with the night-watchman on sailors and their relations. Sailors skip visits, he says, because a railway ticket costs as much as a barrel of beer, and because relations expect presents from half over the world. Relations also mind appearances and collars.

Dress is everything nowadays, the watchman argues. Put him in a top hat and tail-coat, and none could tell him from a lord. A bishop in his clothes would be offered a half-pint. The tale grows from that joke about clothes and kin. Readers get a short, sharp comic monologue, complete on its own.
11188-the-temptation-of-samuel-burge-cap:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short comic tale, The Temptation of Samuel Burge, eighth in the Captains All series. Mr. Higgs, jeweller, sits in the parlour behind his shop, gazing hungrily at a supper-table laid some time before. It is a quarter to ten by the town clock, and Higgs tries to recall what etiquette says about starting a meal before an expected guest arrives.

The housekeeper expects a London gentleman who keeps late hours, and Brother Burge, a selected instrument from the chapel at Clerkenwell, crowded to hear him. Brother Clark wrote that Burge only lives for the work, though Higgs fancies he was a little wild in his younger days. Burge himself asks what a jeweller's shop is compared with a human soul, a priceless human soul. Jacobs turns chapel piety and a jeweller's temptations into gentle comedy.
11478-bedridden-and-the-winter-offensive:
Jacobs's Deep Waters pair Bedridden and The Winter Offensive takes the form of a householder's diary for July 1915, recording billetitis spreading north of King's Road. Entries note Inns of Court men peeping over a gate, Quartermaster-Sergeant Beddem requesting billets with smiles and gulps. A household's capitulation from one billet to two, then three, with heated debate over sheets behind the dining-room door. Night entries log Private Merited still going upstairs at 2:20 a. m.

The Winter Offensive continues the billeting farce. Jacobs, writing during the war, turns the home front into comedy: civilians besieged by soldiers' charm. The diary form suits the material, each entry a small surrender. Readers will enjoy its precise, domestic humor.
12128-a-tiger-s-skin-the-lady-of-the-bar:
A sign painter repainting the Cauliflower inn sign sets off A Tiger Skin, a comic village tale from W. W. Jacobs Lady of the Barge. The oldest man in Claybury, who drank under the old sign for seventy years, tells the painter how the village came to fear a tiger.

A tramp tale of an escaped beast spreads through Claybury, and soon pigs vanish, children claim sightings, and neighbors argue over locked doors and back gates. No one has truly seen the animal, but fear does the tiger work for it. Jacobs builds the joke slowly: rumor, fed by drink and gossip, grows teeth. The story is a neat parable of panic, told in the plain speech of men at a pub table.
12145-the-poetical-works-of-william-word:
William Knight edited this second volume of Wordsworth poetical works, published in 1896 as part of an eight-volume set. The volume covers poems written from 1798 to about 1800, the years of Lyrical Ballads and the poet early maturity.

Readers find Peter Bell, Tintern Abbey, Nutting, the Lucy poems, Lucy Gray, Ruth, Hart-Leap Well, and The Brothers, arranged by year with notes. Wordsworth turns to shepherds, children, ruined cottages, and the Wye valley, arguing that feeling and memory give common life its weight. The edition is scholarly but readable, and it shows the poet moving from ballad experiments toward the meditative voice that made him famous.
12158-the-vigil-night-watches-part-8:
Mr. Farrer calls himself the happiest man in the world, and Miss Ward answers, wait till father comes in. That exchange opens The Vigil, a comic courtship tale from W. W. Jacobs Night Watches.

Ex-Sergeant-Major Ward wants his daughter to marry a soldier, not a soft young man of the present day, and he bursts in on the lovers behind a plant screen. Farrer must then prove his courage, and Ward, in canvas shoes with rubber soles, sets out at night to test him, or frighten him off. Ghost stories crowd Ward mind on the dark road, and the hunter grows more afraid than the hunted. Jacobs turns a father test into a farce of nerves.
12180-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Samuel Richardson epistolary novel Clarissa, first published in 1748, runs to nine volumes, and this eighth volume carries the story toward its close. Told entirely in letters, the novel follows Clarissa Harlowe, a young woman pressed by her family to marry a man she hates.

In this volume Clarissa, ill and worn down, settles her affairs, writes farewell letters, and names Belford her executor, while her family trades blame and Lovelace, her seducer, grows desperate. Miss Howe, Mrs. Norton, and cousin Morden weigh in with counsel and grief. The letters slow the action to a moral reckoning: Clarissa claims her conscience, her family faces its cruelty, and the novel prepares its tragic end.
12208-the-changing-numbers-odd-craft-par:
Mr. Samuel Gunnill creeps downstairs at eight in the morning to face his daughter Selina, and the scene opens The Changing Numbers, a farce from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. Gunnill was bailed out at one in the morning, brought home singing, and now pretends deep interest in window plants.

Selina, courted by the meek Mr. Drill, endures her father antics while a younger rival, Mr. Sims, watches tenderly over the beer jug. The plot turns on swapped numbers, mistaken suitors, and Gunnill bounding about the living room to prove his vigor. Jacobs keeps the comedy domestic: a father who will not grow old gracefully, a daughter who will not be managed, and suitors caught between them.
21212-the-lives-of-the-painters-sculptor:
Giorgio Vasari's Lives is the founding book of art history, and this first of eight volumes covers the earliest Italian masters. It begins with Cimabue and the sculptor Arnolfo, then moves through the Pisani, Giotto, and Andrea Pisano. Simone Martini, Pietro Cavallini, and Ambrogio Lorenzetti close the early ranks.

Vasari's preface argues that design is the creative root of painting, sculpture, and architecture alike, born when God formed man. Each life mixes biography, works, and judgement in Vasari's own order. Readers meet Renaissance art at its source: a painter writing about painters, with strong opinions about who mattered and why.
24256-parochial-and-plain-sermons-vol-vi:
John Henry Newman, formerly vicar of St. Mary's, Oxford, published this seventh volume of his Parochial and Plain Sermons in a new edition with Longmans, Green, and Company in 1891. The set runs to eight volumes, and this one gathers sermons preached to a parish congregation in plain, searching language. Its texts range from Ecclesiastes and Isaiah to the Gospel of John and the First Epistle of John.

Sermons include The Lapse of Time, Religion a Weariness to the Natural Man, The World our Enemy, Mental Prayer, Infant Baptism, The Unity of the Church, and Stedfastness in the Old Paths. The first bids hearers do with all their might the great work of their souls' salvation. Readers get Newman the parish preacher, earnest and direct.
24284-parochial-and-plain-sermons-vol-vi:
John Henry Newman, formerly vicar of St. Mary's, Oxford, published this eighth and last volume of his Parochial and Plain Sermons in a new edition with Longmans, Green, and Company in 1891. Like its fellows, it gathers sermons preached to a parish congregation in plain, searching language, each anchored in a text from scripture. The volume closes a set that taught a generation of Anglicans to hear doctrine in everyday speech.

Sermons include Reverence in Worship, Divine Calls, The Trial of Saul, and The Call of David. Later ones treat Curiosity of Temptation to Sin, Miracles no Remedy for Unbelief, Josiah a Pattern for the Ignorant, and Inward Witness to the Truth of the Gospel. Samuel, Saul, David, and Josiah supply the figures. Readers get Newman the parish preacher at his most direct.
24532-journeys-through-bookland-vol-8:
Charles H. Sylvester compiled this eighth volume of Journeys Through Bookland, a reading plan for children based on the world's best literature. The Chicago edition, published by Bellows-Reeve in 1922, mixes stories, poems, and history retold for young readers. Its contents open with Ringrose and his buccaneers and David Crockett.

Later pieces include Crockett in the Creek War, the retreat of Cortes from Prescott, Macaulay's Battle of Ivry, the Battle of Thermopylae, and Halleck's Marco Bozzaris. Sylvester's plan leads children step by step from adventure to history and poetry. The volume works as both a reader and a guided tour of books worth knowing.
27703-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-septembe:
Buchanan's Journal of Man, volume one, number eight, dated September 1887, continues the editor's anthropological and psychical journal. Its contents list the Concord symposium, the rectification of cerebral science, and human longevity.

Miscellaneous intelligence covers an important discovery, Greek philosophy, the Concord School, new books, solar biology, astronomy, and a mathematical prodigy, with women's rights and progress and co-education. Chapter seven concludes the practical utility of anthropology, and chapter eight treats the origin and foundation of the new anthropology. The Concord symposium piece doubts pedantic scholars who burrow in antiquity and miss the glorious sky overhead. The pages mix science, faith, and fancy. Spirit writing gets a note too. Women's rights get notes too. The range is wide.
31146-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Volume eight of Stories by American Authors, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896, collects five stories. J. W. De Forest opens with The Brigade Commander, in which a colonel is the idol of his bragging regiment and brigade not for goodness or mercy. He leads them to victory and fame, pitiless as he may be.

Henry A. Beers follows with Split Zephyr, Elizabeth Stuart Phelps with Zerviah Hope, Alvey A. Adee with The Life-Magnet, and Elizabeth D. B. Stoddard with Osgood's Predicament. The set gives a compact sample of American magazine fiction of the 1880s, from Civil War command to domestic comedy and strange invention.
32459-the-poetical-works-of-william-word:
William Wordsworth's poems appear here in volume four of eight, edited by William Knight and published in London and New York in 1896. The volume opens its contents with poems dated 1806, including To the Spade of a Friend, Character of the Happy Warrior, The Horn of Egremont Castle, A Complaint, and Stray Pleasures. Later entries include Power of Music, Star-gazers, and the sonnet beginning Nuns fret not at their convent's narrow room.

Knight's edition keeps poetry line markers, notes on variants, and footnotes at chapter ends, with spelling quirks retained and listed. Readers get Wordsworth in his middle years, writing about work, memory, nature, and moral character in plain, musical verse. The volume suits students and lovers of English poetry who want a scholarly, complete text.
4442-vittoria-volume-8:
Book Eight of George Meredith's Vittoria opens through the winter, as Weisspriess and Wilfrid make their way toward Milan together, silently smoking. One attempt at talk touches Vittoria's marriage, and at Monza the officer asks his degraded brother in arms whether he wants leave to serve in Hungary. The war has worn both men down.

The book's chapters promise the interview, the shadow of conspiracy, and the last meeting in Milan. The wife and the husband follow, with many paths converging to the end and an epilogue. This final volume closes Vittoria's story of song, revolt, and marriage, as Italy's struggle and her own reach their close.
4451-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Eight of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with strange revelations, as Harry and his father stand at different windows, watching unconcerned people below. His grandfather has his last outburst, and the heiress proves she inherits the feud, while Harry goes drifting. The adventurer's net begins to tear.

The book's chapters follow Harry's return to England, a meeting with his first playfellow, and his taking of punishment, before the conclusion. Harry at last judges his father clearly, and chooses his own road. This final volume closes the long romance of a boy, a rogue, and a fortune, with feeling and wit.
7161-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-8:
Part eight of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter twenty seven, In Prison, where crowded cells force the two friends to be chained in a large room for trifling offences. Some twenty manacled and fettered prisoners share it, of both sexes and varying ages, an obscene and noisy gang. The king chafes bitterly over the stupendous indignity put upon his royalty, while Hendon stays moody and taciturn.

Hendon feels thoroughly bewildered, having come home a jubilant prodigal expecting wild joy at his return, and instead receiving the cold shoulder and a jail. Promise and fulfillment differ so widely the effect stuns him, and he cannot decide whether it is most tragic or most grotesque. He feels like a man who danced out to enjoy a rainbow and got struck by lightning, before his thoughts settle into order.
7200-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-8:
Part Eight of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer opens on a village still mourning lost children who have not been found. Public prayers and private prayers full of heart have brought no good news from the cave. Most searchers have given up and gone back to daily work, saying the children can never be found. Mrs Thatcher lies very ill, often delirious, calling for her child.

Twain keeps the grief plain and close, letting the town's worry speak through small details rather than grand speech. The cave search hangs over every house, and hope thins with each passing day. This part alone carries the mourning village and the fading search, before the tale turns toward rescue.
7249-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Eight of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee finds London, to a slave, merely a great big village of mud and thatch, its streets muddy, crooked, and unpaved. A drifting swarm of rags and splendours fills them, nodding plumes and shining armour side by side. The king, in rags himself, sees only the outside of his own palace and sighs, swearing a little in a poor juvenile sixth-century way.

Knights and grandees whom the travellers know pass without knowing them, for rags, dirt, and raw welts hide their faces, and it would be unlawful to hail them. Twain's London is a city seen from below, where rank hides in plain sight. This part holds the muddy capital and its unrecognised king.
8478-life-on-the-mississippi-part-8:
Part 8 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 36, The Professor's Yarn, told by a man who was not yet a professor. He was a humble young land surveyor, with the world before him to survey. Under contract to survey a route for a great mining ditch in California, he traveled thither by sea, a voyage of three or four weeks, among many passengers.

This section is Twain's anthology of river talk, where a fellow traveler's yarn takes over the narrative. Readers get a story within the story, with the surveyor's California hopes as its engine. It shows Twain's method: let a character talk, and the book grows by anecdote, one yarn at a time.
8589-roughing-it-part-8:
Part 8 of Mark Twain's Roughing It opens with chapter 71, at four in the afternoon, winding down a mountain of dreary, desolate lava to the sea, closing a pleasant land journey. The lava is the accumulation of ages, torrent after torrent of fire rolling down in old times, building the island structure higher and higher, honeycombed underneath with caves.

This section reaches Hawaii, where Twain's western journey becomes an island visit, with volcanoes, lava fields, and Pacific light. Readers get Twain as traveler in a new landscape, after the deserts and mines of the mainland. Part 8 suits readers following Roughing It to its end, and those who want Twain on Hawaii.
8708-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-8:
This eighth volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery reaches the Passion, opening with Jesus and the woman taken in adultery. Who is set before him in the Temple as the scribes demand a judgment. Mercy answers the trap, and the volume moves on through the resurrection of Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, the Last Supper, and the agony in the garden of Olives. Betrayal, flagellation, and fainting under the cross follow.

The Crucifixion and its close end the sequence, in passages chosen for their visual and emotional weight. Dore's engravings made these scenes famous across the Christian world, and the text preserves the order and emphasis of his selection. Readers can use the volume for Holy Week reflection, or as a compact gospel narrative told in the Bible's own words, scene by scene.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 8 of Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court finds the escaped pair in London, where the king sees his own palace from outside while chained among slaves. the crowd watches a man boiled to death for counterfeiting pennies. A newsboy in the street tells Hank the one cheering fact available: his lieutenant Clarence still keeps the schools, wires, and newspapers alive back at Camelot.

Arrest, a gallows crowd, and a last-minute rescue by Sir Launcelot's knights arriving on bicycles carry the story home in a rush. Hank then answers the knights' challenge with a lasso and revolvers, and the narrative jumps three years. Hank married to Sandy and a father, his new civilization spread across the kingdom, until the Church moves at last against him.
a-tiger-s-skin-the-lady-of-the-barge-and: William Wymark Jacobs tells a comic story in which a travelling sign painter repaints the sign of the Cauliflower at Claybury. The oldest man in the village, who has drunk his beer under that sign for pretty near seventy years, regrets that it could not last his time. Two young gentlemen passing through told the landlord they had sought the Cauliflower and thought the sign a very good likeness of George the Fourth. The painter laughs at the tale.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-8:
Volume eight of the Ante-Nicene Fathers is the set's cabinet of curiosities: the Twelve Patriarchs, excerpts and epistles, the Clementina, apocrypha, decretals, and the Memoirs of Edessa. Roberts and Donaldson edited the volume in 1885. Syriac documents and remains of the first age fill out its pages.

The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs put deathbed wisdom in the mouths of Jacob's sons. The Clementina spin a romance of Peter's travels and debates. The Edessa documents carry the legend of King Abgar, who was said to write to Jesus himself. Much here is legend rather than history, and that is its value: it shows what ordinary early Christians loved to read.
arabian-nights-payne-1884-vol-8:
Volume VIII of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, printed in 1884, stands one step from the end. The Calcutta text's remaining nights pass in John Payne's English, the first complete rendering of the Alf Laylah wa Laylah. Shahrazad's long gamble with the king approaches its reckoning as the tales accumulate.

Eight volumes in, the cycle has covered seas, deserts, and the realms of the jinn many times over. Payne's steady prose keeps faith with the Arabic storytellers' art to the last. Volume VIII sets up the finale of a translation that reshaped what English readers meant by the Arabian Nights.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-8:
Volume eight of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud joins three tractates: Taanith, Megilla, and Ebel Rabbathi. Taanith governs fast days called in drought and danger. Megilla rules the reading of Esther at Purim, and Ebel Rabbathi treats mourning and burial.

On fasts, the rabbis set the order of prayer and the shofar blasts as rain fails. Megilla then turns joyful, fixing how the scroll is read and the feast kept. The mourning tractate closes the volume gravely, with rules for grief, graves, and comfort for the dead's kin. Few volumes show the Talmud's range so plainly in one binding.
bancroft-history-us-vol-8:
Confederation years fill the eighth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1860. Freed from Britain, the states struggle to govern under the loose Articles of Confederation. Debts, disputes, and weak central power plague the fragile new nation.

Bancroft argues that liberty needed order and union to survive. The failures of the 1780s make his case for the Constitution to come. Farmers rebel, states quarrel, and credit sinks in his account. He treats the decade as a stern lesson, not a golden age. The volume closes the main narrative of his democratic epic on a note of warning and hope.
bedridden-and-the-winter-offensive-deep-:
W. W. Jacobs pairs two wartime sketches in this eighth part of Deep Waters. Bedridden runs as a diary from July 1915. An epidemic of Billetitis spreads from the north of King's Road. Inns of Court men peep over the gate, and a quartermaster-sergeant requests an interview. The narrator doses himself with Phospherine and agrees to take a billet before the corps goes under canvas.

His house fills past bearing. Private Early sleeps on the garden seat; Private Merited writes a long, well-reasoned letter to his tailor at the study table and cannot be disturbed. The bathroom door is locked, and a peevish Scotch voice complains of the water's temperature. The Winter Offensive companion piece keeps the same front: the home front, where the invasion is real, billeted, and impossible to escape.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100030001-8:
Survey report titled The CIA Recruitment System: A Survey of Recent Entrants on Duty was conducted by the Office of the Inspector General in August 1979. It is marked Confidential. A letter to new employees states the inspection's purpose: to judge whether recruitment and selection won the quality and numbers of staff the agency needed.

The inspection addressed every part of the process, the letter states: setting personnel needs, finding candidates, and testing, selecting, and processing applicants. Costs were also in scope, agencywide. The enclosed questionnaire was for employees who had entered on duty since 1 October 1977. They were asked about their experiences and views of the process, told not to sign, and promised no attempt to identify individual respondents. Answers were due within two weeks to the Inspector General's office at Headquarters. A separate questionnaire for supervisors came in the same packet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100070007-8:
Inspector General's survey of the Junior Officer Training Program, with its covering memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence, dates to February 1956. Lyman B. Kirkpatrick signed the cover as Inspector General. The survey was made at the specific request of the Deputy Director for Support and the Director of Training, it states.

The survey noted several specific flaws that should be corrected, Kirkpatrick writes. Even so, the Director of Training had done an excellent job setting the program up and developing its basic concepts, he states. Trainees taken in under it had proven outstanding employees. A majority of agency executives agreed it should expand, to provide more staff of that calibre, he reports. A plan for gradual expansion sits inside the report. One recommendation asks the Director of Training to prepare a written brief defining outside consultants' functions in detail. A draft reply for the Director's signature is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100090005-8:
Journal article in the Journal of Applied Psychology, 1969, volume 53, number 6, pages 439 to 445, is by Garland Y. DeNelsky and Michael G. McKee of the CIA. Its title announces a study of how well job performance can be predicted from assessment reports. A modified Q-sort technique is the method at its centre.

Seven psychologists read pre-employment assessment reports for 32 government employees, the abstract states. From them they predicted overall effectiveness plus specific performance and personality traits. They then rated actual effectiveness from the narrative parts of each man's fitness reports. A significant positive link was found between predicted and actual effectiveness, the authors report. The judges also beat base rates on specific traits, they state. The introduction traces assessment research back twenty years, to the 1948 OSS volume Assessment of Men. Results tie judged effectiveness to supervisors' own letter ratings of strong and proficient.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100110002-8:
Pamphlet from BNA Books gathers the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures with supporting material. Its contents are an analysis by Mary Green Miner and John B. Miner, the full text of the guidelines, and questions and answers prepared by a joint government committee. A bibliography on testing closes the volume.

The analysis explains that the guidelines decide whether a selection procedure is unlawful. They were finally agreed by four federal agencies and published in the Federal Register on August 25, 1978, it states. The Civil Service Commission, the Justice Department, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and the Labor Department adopted them jointly. They took effect on September 25, 1978. The guidelines text demands hard evidence for validity claims. Where a study covers a group of jobs, observed work behaviours and products for each must back an assertion, it states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100050009-8:
A mishandled parcel of classified papers is laid out in a confidential memorandum dated 20 June 1983. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to the Chief of the Domestic Security Branch. The Army Center of Military History had reported that a courier package sent on 26 April was not delivered until 31 May, and arrived opened.

The contents were intact, but the outer envelope was gone and the inner one had been unsealed. An Army inquiry traced both the delay and the opening to Army couriers. The account rests on word from Special Agent John Hott of the 902nd Military Intelligence Group. The papers were 28 classified items, ten top secret and eighteen secret, sent to an Army historian.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100070007-8:
Where the CIA History Staff should sit inside the Agency is argued at length in a memorandum dated 19 October 1983. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to the Executive Director and makes the case that the staff must stay independent, inside the Office of the Director. Proposals to move or merge it had been raised that summer.

Two questions are taken in turn: moving the staff into one of the four directorates, and folding it into other offices dealing with history or study. McDonald recalls that both points were weighed in 1980 when the staff was revived. He notes the staff has sat in the Director's office since Walter Bedell Smith set it up in 1951.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-01773r000200400001-8:
Possible photographs for a CIA history volume are listed by name in a file tied to The CIA and Congress, Volume I, Early Oversight 1947-1965. No narrative text appears. The list runs to dozens of names under a Senate heading, followed by a House list.

Senators named include Richard Russell, Carl Hayden, Joseph McCarthy, Mike Mansfield, and Lyndon Johnson, along with committee staff such as William Darden. The House list begins with Clarence Cannon and John Taber and runs through senior figures of the early oversight years. Read as a working tool, the list shows which faces the history's editors thought might illustrate the first two decades of congressional dealings with the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100100026-8:
Names and clearances for a briefing symposium are forwarded in a memorandum for the record dated 4 March 1985. The subject is a symposium of briefings on National Security Decision Directive 145, set for 15 March 1985. Three Agency officers are listed as its representatives, from the Office of Information Technology and the Intelligence Community Staff.

Their clearances went to the Security Officer at the Institute for Defense Analyses. Attached is a February 1985 letter from the National Security Agency to John McMahon. It recalls that the President signed NSDD 145 on 17 September 1984, setting national policy on telecommunications and automated information systems security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100150003-8:
Catalogued under a handwritten label, the hosted text is National Security Decision Directive 273, United States Policy Toward South Africa, issued in 1987 and signed for the President by Frank Carlucci. Routing slips and a National Security Council handling notice precede the directive. The text builds on an earlier directive, NSDD 187 of September 1985.

The directive reviews what had changed since 1985: a state of emergency from June 1986, harsher repression, failed Commonwealth peace efforts, and cross-border military action. It describes the African National Congress turning more to political and diplomatic work while still backing violence. Sanctions and strained ties with Washington also figure. The stated course is active engagement toward a nonracial democracy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100160002-8:
National Security Decision Directive 319, United States Policy Towards Indochina, is approved in a White House memorandum dated 14 November 1988. The note goes to the Vice President and the heads of State and Defense, the Director of Central Intelligence, and the Joint Chiefs chairman. The directive rests on a national security study of October 1988.

Its background cites Vietnamese pledges to leave Cambodia and wider talks on a settlement. Approved steps include closer talks with ASEAN states and continued economic isolation of Vietnam. The United States would back Prince Sihanouk, oppose any return of the Khmer Rouge to power, and tie warmer gestures toward Vietnam to progress on Cambodia and on prisoner and missing-man issues.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900030004-8:
Spare parts for one compressor family are catalogued in an Ingersoll-Rand parts list dated January 1979, replacing an April 1977 edition. The list covers ESV non-lubricated portplate type compressors. A front table ties machine sizes, from 6 by 5 up to 9-1/2 by 7, to serial designations and valve sizes for inlet and discharge.

Ordering instructions ask buyers to go through the nearest parts and service distributor. Orders must give the model and serial number from the nameplate, the booklet form number, and the quantity and reference number for each part. Three classes of recommended spares are set out, from a minimum set for domestic service to a maximum set for export.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100040001-8:
Guyana after the Grenada intervention is assessed in a secret intelligence paper dated February 1984, ALA 84-10012. The Office of African and Latin American Analysis led the work, with help from Soviet, Near Eastern, and East Asian analysis offices. Coordination with the operations directorate is noted on the title pages.

The body weighs economic and political prospects under President Burnham. One thread is pressure from international financial bodies for a freer private sector. The paper argues that such freedom would quickly help some trading communities while cutting into the standing of Burnham's own base, which made the issue one he would not bargain over. Foreign private investment is shown as the one area where he signaled room to move.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100310001-8:
Mexico's foreign policy under President de la Madrid is reviewed in a Directorate of Intelligence memorandum dated 4 May 1984. The National Security Council's senior Latin America staffer requested the paper. It rests on information available as of 3 May 1984 and was coordinated with the operations directorate.

The summary says de la Madrid has dropped his predecessor's confrontational style and played down foreign issues at home. Long-standing invitations to visit Nicaragua and Cuba went unanswered, likely to avoid offending Washington. Newer steps, such as financial aid to Argentina and a trip through South America, signal a wider hemispheric reach. The paper reports the trip strengthened ties with key South American governments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100400001-8:
Nicaraguan support for unrest in the region is tracked in a Directorate of Intelligence memorandum dated 19 September 1984. Robert McFarlane, the President's national security adviser, requested the paper. Analysts in the Middle America-Caribbean Division prepared it. The operations directorate coordinated the work.

The summary reports that Nicaragua keeps backing armed revolt against non-Marxist governments. Help takes the form of arms, training, radio support, and advice. Salvadoran guerrillas remain the main recipient. Costa Rican and Honduran groups have also been helped. Evidence points to a steady flow of arms and men to El Salvador, at times in large amounts. A rise in Cuban weapons deliveries from April is also noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302190001-8:
Japan's Socialists under a new chairman are weighed in a memorandum dated 5 November 1984. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available as of 2 November. Masashi Ishibashi took charge of the Japan Socialist Party in September 1983. He inherited a divided party that was losing ground with voters.

His reply was a call for a new start for the largest opposition party. Better ties with the United States sit at the center of his plan. Other foreign policy moves support the same aim: to soften the party's leftist image. The paper credits him with some progress. It also notes his balancing act. He must hold the left and right wings together, without drifting so far to the center that the party loses its identity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302280001-8:
Thailand's currency devaluation and the storm around it are covered in a memorandum dated 30 November 1984. The paper rests on information available as of 29 November. A surprise 17 percent devaluation took effect on 5 November, moving the rate from 23 to 27 baht per dollar.

Prime Minister Prem defused political and military opposition with skill, the paper judges, and came out stronger at the expense of his chief rival, Armed Forces Commander General Athit. Prem had resisted such a step for over a year despite a record trade deficit of 3.9 billion dollars in 1983. Fresh attacks are expected over the austerity steps meant to back the devaluation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200860001-8:
Chinese work on advanced composite materials is examined in a secret research paper dated July 1985, EA 85-10131. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it. The subtitle points to strategic implications, and the paper treats the materials as a military question from the start.

China has run a major effort since at least 1979 to build an advanced composites industry, the paper reports. Such materials could sharpen the design of advanced weapons. The body tracks gear China seeks or has bought abroad, such as pultrusion machines sold by a British firm. Test gear is also listed: acoustic emission systems, materials analysis systems, and machines that measure stress in cured composites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201300001-8:
Japan news for February 1985 is rounded up in a confidential memorandum dated 26 February 1985. The Japan Branch prepared it, using information available that day. It carries the number EA M 85-10041 and a duplicate file note.

Opposition parties halted the lower house budget committee three times during the month. Prime Minister Nakasone made disputed statements on defense and tax policy, and broke a postwar taboo by attending National Foundation Day rites on 11 February. Yet the press gave top billing to a new group, the Sosei-kai, formed by Finance Minister Takeshita. Party officials call it a policy study group; press reports say it bears the marks of a faction.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201490001-8:
Southwest China's economy is profiled in a memorandum dated 4 April 1985, built around the Chengdu Consular District. The district takes in Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, and Tibet. Tables inside sum up each province and its largest cities.

The four provinces hold a stated share of China's people just above their share of farm and industrial output value. Sichuan, the most populous province, is the clear economic center. Its city of Chongqing, at 13.9 million people in total, is now China's biggest, ahead of Shanghai. Chengdu, the provincial capital and consulate seat, counts 8.5 million. Kunming in Yunnan is the only other large city named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201580001-8:
United States-China economic relations are reviewed in a memorandum dated 19 April 1985. The summary opens with a fall: in two years the United States has dropped to third place as a supplier to China, behind Japan and Hong Kong. China is still one of the fastest growing markets for American technology and services.

Trade will not reach its full size unless a host of shared issues are handled well, the paper judges. Textile disputes head the list. A bilateral investment treaty is blocked, shipping talks show no sign of return, and a nuclear cooperation pact stays in suspense. An airline permit problem must be faced before May. Export control demands and Asian Development Bank membership also rankle.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201670001-8:
Foreign investment in China is mapped in a memorandum dated 17 May 1985. The summary counts the boom since 1979: more than 2,100 joint ventures, cooperative firms, and wholly foreign-owned businesses have been set up. Paid-in foreign investment reached 3.7 billion dollars by the end of 1984.

That total is still far short of China's needs, the paper says, and Beijing will seek much more during the Seventh Five-Year Plan. Transport, communications, and energy are top needs, all fields where American firms compete well, so they should gain from the modernization drive. Slow early progress is blamed on mixed signals from leaders, thin rules on taxes, weak infrastructure, and low labor productivity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301930001-8:
Key Chinese policymakers on a bilateral investment treaty are profiled in a memorandum dated 22 July 1985, EA M-85-10137. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, using information available that day. Decision making on the treaty is centralized, the summary says, and the main actors are named one by one.

Most of China's economic leaders favor a treaty with the United States, but they will not grant large concessions to get one, the paper reports. Few think a signed treaty would spark a surge in American investment. Its worth is seen as political: proof that China's reforms can be trusted. Premier Zhao heads the profiles as the top administrative authority on economic affairs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302100001-8:
Hong Kong land policy under the Sino-British Joint Declaration is explained in a memorandum dated 16 September 1985, EAM-10164-85. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, using information available that day. Land was one of the hottest points in last year's talks on Hong Kong's future.

Britain agreed to a joint commission to watch over land policy during the transition. The Hong Kong government keeps day-to-day control but under new limits. It may auction no more than 50 hectares a year, and half of sales revenue must go to a fund held for the post-1997 government. Only the joint commission can lift the land cap or spend the fund on projects before 1997.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302380001-8:
Cuba's offer to pull military personnel out of Nicaragua is examined in a memorandum dated 8 March 1985 for the Director of Central Intelligence. Latin American analysts prepared the paper. Cover notes dated 11 March 1985 send it to the national intelligence officers for Africa and Latin America.

Havana's pledge to recall 100 military personnel starting in May is judged mainly a propaganda ploy. It backs Nicaraguan efforts to build pressure on the Reagan administration, the paper argues. A parallel is drawn with Angola in 1976, when the Cuban troop presence peaked at 36,000. Withdrawal talk then came only once the battlefield favored Havana, and the paper finds no evidence it aimed at American lawmaking.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100160002-8:
Pages from a Supreme Court opinion in See v. City of Seattle make up a legal text held in Agency files. The passage reproduced covers the end of the opinion, section IV. The case concerns a man charged with a crime for refusing to let housing inspectors enter his leasehold without a warrant.

The Court notes there was no emergency: inspectors came three times seeking consent, and no warrant was ever obtained. Entry into the public part of the building, with the landlord's consent, did not authorize inspection of the tenant's own premises. The holding gives the tenant a constitutional right to insist on a warrant, and bars conviction for refusing the search. Citations to earlier search cases support the ruling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200490009-8:
Vincent Davis asks Stansfield Turner to clear a speaking invitation in a letter dated 18 January 1980. An invitation is attached to the letter. Davis wants it run by Turner first. The speaker sought is a man named John. His talk for a Naval Reserve group in Columbus the past September went over so well.

Davis wants almost the same talk in Lexington. The crowd there is a different kind, with strong public impact. He also asks for 250 more copies of the unclassified report, if they can be spared. The speaker can expect far better local hospitality than Columbus allowed, he adds. Turner himself is urged to return for the Board of Advisors meetings. Those meetings fall on 11 and 12 April.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040005-8:
DCI Schedules, November 1977 starts with a topic index. It groups the Director's actions under Angola, leaks, and the Middle East. MKULTRA, oversight, and personnel appear too. So do the State Department and tactical versus national intelligence. The index lists a record of an NSC staff meeting on Angola. It lists testimony and discussion records on leaks. Letters concerning Columbia University appear. So does a draft presentation script on personnel cuts. The script was made for the Senate intelligence committee.

Daily appointment pages follow. They record briefings for the President. They also record meetings with Dr. Brzezinski. Sessions on the Helms case and talks on the budget appear. A warning-indicator briefing is logged too. David Aaron had requested that briefing. As with the other months in this series, redactions appear throughout. They run through all the released pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401150003-8:
Trip New York and Atlanta, 5-6 October 1977 papers, the third of three files, preserve one meeting record. It covers the Council on Foreign Relations meeting of 5 October 1977, held in Turner's honor. The program gives his talk's title, "Secrecy and Morality in Intelligence." It gives the hour. It names McGeorge Bundy, president of the Ford Foundation, as presiding officer. Pages of member and staff names follow. So does the Council's rule against attributing statements made in its meetings.

Speaking notes weigh two dangers. Both dangers grow out of the new oversight climate. One is timidity, and the other is security leaks. The notes describe Turner's effort to write a code of ethics. The code was meant for the intelligence community. It was modeled in part on industry examples. Other themes are public oversight and wider sharing, within the limits of secrecy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401170001-8:
Trip to Illinois and Indiana, 11-14 November 1977 is a very large file. It records the Director's Midwest speaking trip. Planning memos route Turner from Indianapolis to DePauw University. He gave an address and attended a luncheon there. The route ran on to Wabash College and Chicago engagements. Those included the Council on Foreign Relations. A 15 November memo went to the National Intelligence Officer for the Near East and South Asia. It passes along two Chicago contacts. They had discussed Indian politics with Turner. They might consult on an estimate.

Press coverage reports his DePauw speech. It was his first speech to students as Director. In it, he named timidity and leaks as the two risks. Both risks came with the new oversight system. He voiced optimism about the balance being struck. Thank-you letters and enclosures round out the papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501230003-8:
Meritorious Unit Citation (Sanitized) is a thin planning file. Its main paper is a DCI planning item received 20 September 1979. The item came from the Honor and Merit Award Board. It proposed that the Director present a Meritorious Unit Citation. The event would be at CIA Headquarters, in the week of 29 October 1979. A suspense date of 25 September was set for the decision.

The form's boxes are largely unmarked in the sanitized copy. The boxes cover the aide's recommendation, and any added attendees. They also cover the Director's decision: schedule, decline, or see me. The unit to be honored is not named. A blank routing and transmittal slip from September 1977 is kept in the file too. Its remarks are illegible handwriting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501250001-8:
September and October 1978 press clippings make up a CIA news file. The agency saved print from those two months. An early Los Angeles Times piece makes a case for spy work. It says the spy services must keep the country aware of threats. Plots, drug ships and shifts in Soviet talks are its proof.

Other pages cover the death of a CIA man named Paisley. His boat held live shells. So did his flat. Police and old work mates were still probing his loss. The run of cuttings shows the press in two minds. It weighs the worth of spy work against fresh doubt about the agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501340001-8:
January 1979 press clippings fill a CIA file of that month. Forms at the front note stock moved in 2002. The stock went to the declassification center. A trade paper is dated 15 January 1979. It sits under a head for CIA books and studies. It reports a CIA study on Soviet trade. Soviet buys of western machines drove growth, the study found.

Later pages look back at the deaths at Jonestown. They weigh claims the agency slipped up on Iran. It had once helped restore the Shah there. Draft spy charters fill more space. So does Congress oversight. The month paired trade themes with hard tests of the past.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400021-8:
Dated 5 April 1979, a staff note numbered 41 brings a change. Turner and Frank Carlucci set up a CIA Executive Committee. The note tells staff why. The pair wanted a whole-agency view on choices put to them. Staff work alone did not give that view. The new body takes the place of the Executive Advisory Group.

Membership spans the deputy chiefs. Each branch of the house sits on it. Other senior staff sit too. A second part names an outside panel. The panel will audit finished spy work. It will check the fairness of that work. The note shows a director reshaping top review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400049-8:
Two steps to reshape the spy world's top fill this note. It is dated 18 October 1977 and numbered 13. Both steps flow from White House choices on the spy services. On 3 October a tasking center gained its first chief. The center is the National Intelligence Tasking Center. On 11 October two arms merged.

The analytic arm joined the national estimates staff. The merged body is the National Foreign Assessment Center. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, names the men to head each body. The tasking hub should align what all arms gather, he says. A warm close praises the graphics branch. Its night work in aid of the President drew praise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601420083-8:
Nathan A Talbot wrote to Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, on 8 May 1978 in warm thanks. Talbot was an editor in Boston. He worked at the Christian Science Publishing Society. His letter replies to praise from Turner. Turner had praised an editorial on spying. The editorial was called What To Do About Spying.

Talbot wishes the director well in his work. He invites him to call in when next in Boston. The file also holds Turner's own letter. It is dated 27 April 1978. The full text of the editorial sits with them. It treats spying through faith and right thought. The exchange shows a spy chief and a church paper in accord.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601430028-8:
Soviet harassment of Americans gives this press interview its headline theme. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, spoke with editors of The San Diego Union in an exclusive sitting. He pointed to fresh signs of Soviet pressure against the United States. Cases in Moscow drew his fire: reporters and businessmen harassed, a KGB tunnel found in the embassy, and harsh prison terms in trials of dissidents.

The talk ranges wider in question and answer form. Turner fields points on secrecy pledges for past staff, citing the case of a former officer who had signed such a pledge on joining. He treats the pledge as a fair term of service. The clipping shows a director making his case in public, in plain terms, at a tense point in the cold war.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601430037-8:
America's intelligence capability opens this speech as a cornerstone of national security. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, tells his audience that such a talk would once have been out of the question. Spy work was not talked of in past years, he says. Vietnam and Watergate changed that, driving spy work into the headlines.

Allegations, probes and books by former agents followed in a rush. The speech argues that the spy services now work more in the open than at any past point. Turner points to watchdogs set up to guard the law: a board that can hear any complaint and report to the President. He points to two new panels in Congress as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601430046-8:
About Town Hall of California fills a short file on a Los Angeles civic forum. The text calls Town Hall a meeting place for the informed. It calls it a stage for timely themes and a show of facts and views. Leaders in management, labor, government and the schools speak there.

Members can meet the speakers and give their own views. Those too busy to attend can read the Journal or the Reporter for a round-up of what was said. Luncheons with noted guests form the core of the program. The file, kept by the Central Intelligence Agency, is a plain guide to how the forum ran and what it offered its members in that era.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460043-8:
The Courier-Journal of Louisville fills this file as a full day's paper. It is dated Saturday, June 24, 1978. The front guide lists the day's parts: Accent, sports, comics and the marketplace. A Miss America item leads the inside notes, with the title holder in town.

Sports pages carry a Kentucky all-star loss to Indiana. Deaths, racing and TV listings fill their set places. The paper came out on the weekend of the Golden Plate awards in Owensboro. Its presence in the file marks the local press cover of that event. As a record, it is a whole newspaper kept page by page in agency files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470015-8:
Aspen Institute workshop papers set out a week on the ethics of public secrecy. The workshop ran from July 24 to 28, 1978. Graham Allison chaired the Monday talks. The first theme was the pull between openness and secrecy. Harlan Cleveland and others opened that debate.

Tuesday took up the case for secrecy in statecraft, then in spy work. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, himself was listed to speak on the spy side. Later days treat secrecy in arms and in war plans. Each block names a chair and set speakers. The agenda shows a full week built around one hard theme: when a free state may keep secrets, and why.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480041-8:
Turner wrote to Williamson Murray on 21 November 1977 in warm reply. He thanks Murray for a letter of October 12. Murray plainly enjoys Ohio State, Turner notes. Military history is well received there, which pleases him. A check of the schedule opens two dates: the 12th or 13th of April.

Staff would work out the details if either date suits. Turner thanks him too for an article on British strategy toward Italy in the late 1930s. Murray's points on short-term, accurate forecasts are right on the mark, he says. The agency is concentrating on forecasts months ahead, not years, he adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601500011-8:
John W Burke Jr anchors this Business Council file from Washington. Burke served as executive secretary of the council. The file opens with the council's letterhead and a long roll of active members. Chiefs of great banks, car firms and phone companies fill the list.

Guest sketches fill much of the pack. One traces a food company chief born in Antwerp and schooled in Paris. Another traces a law man who became a state attorney general. A guest guide to The Homestead in Virginia closes the file, with notes on dress and trails. The pack served the council's May meeting at Hot Springs, which the Director of Central Intelligence was set to attend.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601510010-8:
Thirty-second Williamsburg Conference of the Aerospace Industries Association fills this pamphlet. The dates are May 24, 25 and 26, 1978. The pamphlet is for the personal information of industry delegates and invited guests. It replaces earlier sheets sent with the invitation letters.

An index maps the parts: general information, the conference schedule, transport, and the speaking program. The association hosts the meeting at Williamsburg. Guests are told to stop at the office in the Inn for more material on arrival. The file is the delegate's handbook for a set-piece meet of the aerospace trade, at which the Director of Central Intelligence was a guest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040002-8:
Face the Nation transcript fills this file from a Sunday broadcast. CBS aired the show on March 20, 1977, late in the morning. The guest was Admiral Stansfield Turner, the new Director of Central Intelligence. Reporters were George Herman, Bob Woodward and Fred Graham.

Mary O Yates produced the show for CBS News. The transcript prints the full half hour of questions and answers. Turner had been in the post for days, not months. The file shows his first big television test: a spy chief on open air, pressed on the trade he had just taken over, in the first spring of a new administration.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200560004-8:
Thomas J Kane Jr wrote on October 23, 1980 from Grumman in Bethpage, New York. Kane was a vice president of the firm. He had read Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,'s recent article in U.S. Naval Proceedings with interest. The article treated the future makeup of the surface fleet. Grumman papers go with the letter.

A brochure and two papers argue for one course of action. The scheme rests on new technology: a ship built to launch missiles and aircraft. The ship is feasible, the firm holds. Missiles exist, with new types in work. The file is a builder's pitch to a naval chief turned spy chief, on the fleet's future shape.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660003-8:
Secretarial-clerical concerns fill this memo routed through the house in 1977. It goes to the Special Assistant to the DCI, by way of the acting deputies for administration. A routing slip heads the file. The memo works through the concerns item by item.

One item treats the vacancy notice system. Office heads were told to guard its fairness, the text says. All employees must have access to the notices. Posting on central boards joins that fix. Career counselors can help staff plan from the notices. Training draws strong support from the group in a later item. The file is the clerical ranks' case, answered point by point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660012-8:
Day care center study moves through this Central Intelligence Agency file on routing and record sheets. The sheets carry the study through the administration arm in late 1978. Officers' comments fill the columns in the set form. The study itself treats space above all.

No space stood free, the study finds. A list of needs for work space ran past 70,000 square feet. A center would need special toilets, a kitchen and nap rooms. A safe outdoor play area would be needed too. Fire, safety and egress rules all bear on the plan. The file is the house study of child care for staff, with the hard facts of room and rules.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680001-8:
Minutes of the Director of Central Intelligence and MAG meeting with Admiral Turner fill this file. The sitting took place on Monday 16 May 1977 at 1715 hours. It is marked for internal use only. Turner sat with the members of his management advisory group. A chairman and a recording secretary are named.

Personal introductions opened the meeting. The chairman then reviewed the agenda. An overview of the group's concept followed. How the group would work, and what it was for, filled that part. The minutes show the first formal session of a new channel: working staff, picked to advise the director in person, setting out their charter in his presence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780028-8:
Sturdy Stan at the Central Intelligence Agency is the piece this newspaper file was kept for. The paper is The Washington Star of Monday, November 27, 1978. Section C carries amusements and finance. TV tonight leads the sampled pages. Two new series about high school coaches get the critic's eye that night.

Comedy and sport fill the section around the kept piece. The file holds the Star's pages whole, as they came off the press. Their presence in the director's records marks the day a hometown paper profiled its spy chief under a nickname of respect. The record is the issue itself, kept page by page.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300850001-8:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) trip to Boston from 29 November to 1 December 1978 fills this trip book. An outline lists its parts by letter. Schedule comes first. Then come the head table for a World Affairs Council luncheon, and the guests for a Harvard dinner. A World Affairs Council breakfast guest list follows.

A biography of President Derek Bok of Harvard has its own tab. Talking points for talks with Bok fill three more tabs. Boston area contacts and correspondence come next. Newspaper clips close the book, with more to come on arrival. The schedule shows a Wednesday evening flight from National Airport to Logan, then the Hyatt Regency in Cambridge.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300890007-8:
FIA progress report sums up the Forging Industry Association's year for 1977 to 1978. Robert W Atkinson, executive vice president and treasurer, signs the front note. The report gives an official summation of the association's actions. It highlights trends in the forging industry as well. Conclusions are drawn from each.

Members are urged to keep the reports as a reference series. Formal education and small business efforts lead the sampled text. The report casts the association's role as expanding, and its stature as growing. The file came to the Director of Central Intelligence with the papers of a group that had sought him as a speaker that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300940001-8:
Assembly resolutions for a 1979 annual meeting fill this Dallas file. The resolutions were to be considered at 2:00 p.m. on Monday, August 13. The place was the theater of the Dallas Convention Center. Dorothy Frooks of New York heads the sampled text. Her resolution fights a bill in Congress.

The bill would draft women for military service. The resolution calls it unnecessary and dictatorial. It would deprive a woman of freedom of choice, the text says. Women volunteered in both world wars in large numbers, it notes: 12,500 in the first, about 450,000 in the second. The file, kept in Central Intelligence Agency records, holds the meeting's resolutions in draft form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090022-8:
Pace University fills this file with its schools and degrees in list form. Dyson College of Arts and Sciences leads the roll. The Lubin School of Business Administration follows. The College of White Plains, the School of Education and the Lienhard School of Nursing come next. A graduate school and a school of law close the list.

Degrees run from associate to master level in the pages. Arts, science, business and professional studies all appear. The file is the university's own catalog of parts, kept with the commencement papers of 1980. It shows the shape of the school Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, addressed: many colleges under one name.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140034-8:
Herbert E Hetu wrote to Albert E Cunliff on 23 February 1980 for the Director. Hetu spoke for Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, in his public affairs role. He thanks Cunliff for a letter of February 21. Cunliff had invited Turner to speak at the 1980 Backstoppers fall meeting. The cause is worthy, Hetu grants.

Present plans do not call for the Admiral to make that trip, the letter says. The reply is a regret in the set form of the office: thanks, praise for the cause, and a plain no. The file shows the public affairs desk at its daily work, answering the flood of invitations with courtesy and care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150042-8: A scheduling item for the Director of Central Intelligence scheduling item 80-91 logs an awards ceremony for Monday 21 April 1980. A letter from Ray S Cline brought the item, received on 31 March. Cline would receive an award for the best scholarly article from the National Intelligence Study Center. Hours were 1730 to 1930. The place was the International Club Building on K Street in Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401160032-8:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-145 logs an evening of music and awards for Friday 13 June 1980. An invitation card brought it, received on 20 May. The occasion honored exceptional service and work to end poverty in America. Friends of VISTA hosted the night. Rosalynn Carter gave it honorary sponsorship.

The hour was 2030 that Friday. A suspense date of 23 May is marked on the form. The file is the staff sheet for a charity evening in the Carter years. Volunteers were honored and music was laid on. The spy chief was asked to lend his name to a cause of service at home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401170022-8:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item for March 1981 logs an address ask from Andrew B Sides Jr. The item was received on 27 August 1980, numbered 80-217. The event was an address to the Worcester Economic Club in Worcester, Massachusetts. A mid-week day in March 1981 was wanted. Hours would run from 1800 to 2130.

A suspense date of 10 September 1980 is marked. Sides had pursued the director for the forging industry before. Here he writes for another club in another state. The file is the staff sheet for a far-ahead booking: a dinner club, an evening slot, and a director whose term would end before the date arrived.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401310008-8:
Education program gets a confidential memorandum for the Director dated 1 May 1980. The writer reports a talk of more than an hour with a man named Barry. Barry grasped the problems well, the memo says. The chief problem is leanness: the agency runs thin in people. That thinness tells on students as well.

Doing more with the program would not come easily, the writer warns. A basic assumption is urged on the Director. The scan of the memo is rough in places, but its drift is clear. The file is an internal plea on schooling for staff: aims are agreed, hands are few, and the plan must fit that hard fact.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501350003-8:
Press clippings for the week of 29 February fill this file. An Economist piece of 23 February 1980 leads the sampled pages. Its theme is the bid to recloak Uncle Sam: the administration's effort to restore secrecy around spy work. A file head names Snepp, the former officer whose book had fought the agency in court.

Charter bills run through the week's pages as well. So does the hostage crisis in Iran. The bundle shows a week when three threads crossed: a court fight over a book, a law fight over charters, and a crisis abroad. The agency kept them together as one week's reading for its chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501360002-8:
Press clippings for March 1980 open with a New York Times piece of 3 March. Get it in Writing From the CIA is its head. It treats a message from intelligence chief Stansfield Turner to the Senate. Charter bills fill the file's early pages, as they filled the month. The agency's rules were being written into bills that spring.

Later pages range over Iran and the wider world. The hostage crisis still ran, and Afghanistan still burned in print. The file is a month's bundle in the agency's own keeping: law at home and crisis abroad, cut from the papers day by day and filed as one record of March 1980.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501370001-8:
Press clippings for April 1980 open with editorials around the country. The Atlanta Constitution of 25 March 1980 leads the sampled pages. Central Intelligence Agency and Congress work together is its head. Two extreme schools of thought open its argument. The file gathers editorial pages from many towns on one theme.

Charter bills and oversight drive the month in print. Some papers urged trust; others urged chains. April also closed with a rescue bid in Iran that would fill May's pages. In this bundle the month still belongs to the law fight: how a republic should hold its secret service, argued in the plain words of hometown papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501470028-8:
HMS Bristol is the subject of a short Royal Navy booklet held in Agency files and released in 2009. Pages give the ship as a guided missile destroyer built by Swan Hunter at Wallsend-on-Tyne. She was laid down in April 1967 and launched in 1969, the booklet states.

A full page profiles Captain D. W. Brown, who took command in 1978 as his eighth command. His past posts at sea and ashore are listed in brief. Further pages describe the operations room, weapons control, radio links, and life for 29 officers and 378 ratings. The booklet reads as a ship's own guide for guests and crew.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501540002-8:
Program D-Prime, a civil defence plan, is broken into costed parts in a Federal Emergency Management Agency paper dated 14 December 1979. A chart sets ten work items into five rising packages. The packages run from paper plans alone up to full attack shelter plans and warning work.

Costs climb across the five steps as more items are added. Shelter surveys, shelter stocks, warning, and drill work each carry a share of the total. A model of a heavy mid-1980s attack is used to count who might live or die. Results contrast a weak current program with the fuller D-Prime outcome in stark terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601680051-8:
Outcomes from the 1976 security reinvestigation program are summed up in a memo dated 1 July 1977. Robert W. Gambino, Director of Security, wrote to the Director for information only. The memo answers a 1 June 1977 query on what became of cases that raised concern.

Case results are sorted into lettered groups in attached tabs. Groups cover drug problems, foreign contacts, leaks of secret material, marital strain, drink, money trouble, and rule breaches, among others. Gambino warns that cases often mix several problems at once. Closing pages urge early help from first-line supervisors and wider use of repeat polygraph checks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t02051r000200280010-8:
William P. Bishop gives Senate testimony on satellite data sales in a statement dated 22 March 1984. Bishop chairs the Commerce board judging bids for civil space remote sensing. He speaks for the administration on three bills named the Land Remote Sensing Satellite Authorization Acts.

A request for bids went out on 3 January 1984 and replies came in on 19 March 1984, he states. Bishop stresses he has not read the bids, so his views rest on board work alone. He backs fast sale of the land sensing system to private firms. Points of dispute include who owns the data and who sets its price.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100030001-8:
Economic tables comparing NATO and the Sino-Soviet bloc fill a handbook dated 26 February 1957. The volume is research aid CIA/RR RA-12 from the Office of Research and Reports. Front notes warn that border shifts over 25 years make long runs of data hard to match.

Figures are rounded to three key digits in most tables, the notes state. One table counts horses in 1938 and from 1946 to 1955 by country. It shows steep war losses and slow recovery in bloc states such as Poland and Hungary. Footnotes flag plan figures, gaps, and cases where no output cannot be split from no data.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100120001-8:
United States and Soviet gross national product are matched in a report dated March 1966. The report, CIA/RR ER 66-6, came from the Office of Research and Reports. It covers the years 1955 to 1964 and the main uses of output in each land.

Method pages explain the hard task of pricing Soviet output in dollars. Ruble to dollar ratios are built, checked for bias, and raised in set cases with reasons given. Later pages compare total size, end uses, and state policy outlays. A closing part contrasts the new figures with past estimates of the same match.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-02247r000200190002-8:
Geography of Central Asia, drawn from a work titled The Soviet Union Today, fills an information report card file. Rivers of the region open the text, with the Syr Darya called the Nile of Turkestan. Its flow is put at 3.5 cubic miles a year.

The Amu Darya is given a far larger flow of 10.5 cubic miles a year. Pages trace its old shifts of course since about A.D. 600 and the lost Usboi branch. Heat, sand, and old canal traces shape the account of the Kara Kum desert. Later pages turn to a new canal and its silt and seepage faults.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m00666r000503450007-8:
Claims by Mohammed Reggab about Marina Oswald are weighed in Commission No. 4, dated March 1964. Reggab, a Moroccan student in West Berlin, came forward on 26 November 1963. He spoke to the Satellite Refugee Screening Center four days after the Kennedy killing.

Reggab stated he knew a Marina Nikolaeva in Moscow while he studied film there from 1960 to 1962. He told of dances at Patrice Lumumba University and dates in early 1961. Checks that followed cast doubt on the tale in the findings. Press facts showed Mrs. Oswald had never lived in Moscow, the summary notes. A promised letter and photo from Morocco never arrived by mid-January 1964.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100010005-8:
Public letters by Bishop von Galen against Nazi killing of the sick open a wartime file of mixed papers. A pastoral letter of German churches dated 6 July is quoted at length. Von Galen's third sermon in the set charges that patients taken from homes for the insane were killed.

The file is catalogued with situation reports on Greece, Turkey, and the Balkans from 1944. Later pages held here turn to New York waterfront hiring and sabotage risk. A report there urges an end to the shape-up hiring hall system. It warns that Axis agents could gain dock work with ease under that system. The scan is rough in places but the main texts can be read.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100210003-8:
French-language notes on a go-between open a file catalogued under four heads for the war years. Heads listed name a Four Power Pact note, Europe after Hitler's fall, French leadership after the fall of France, and letters on Otto Strasser. The opening note profiles Marcel Ribardiere in French at length.

Ribardiere is drawn as a Paris business lawyer who grew rich fixing hard trade cases. Travel in Russia, Germany, Belgium, and Italy fed his taste for statecraft, the note states. He posed to each side as the trusted ear of the other, it reports. Later pages turn to sharp personal letters in English, though much of that text is rough in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100450007-8:
Italian diplomacy after the armistice is assessed in reports sent to General Donovan. Major John J. McDonough forwards reports numbered III and IV with fresh detail. They treat the stance of Italian envoys and counsellors in various lands, the covering note states.

Finland pages report that Badoglio felt bound to keep an envoy in Helsinki. Switzerland had been asked to take charge of Italian interests there, the report states. Hungary is said to have known the royal regime only under German pressure. The legation at Rome stands closed in the account, with no envoy sent to the Fascist regime. Later pages turn to Italian hopes and the weight of outside views on the land.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070004-8:
Delivery schedules form an addendum to AQUATONE planning papers in this untitled file. Base completion is marked as June 1955 at the head of the page. All items are to be ready for use one week after delivery, the note states.

Aircraft deliveries run from 25 July 1955 to 6 November 1956 for twenty planes. Engine schedules split between J-57/P-37 and J-57/P-31 types across 1955 to 1957. Camera sets are listed by type, A-1, A-2, B, and C, with monthly dates. Electronic gear follows, with System 1 sets in X-band and S-band lines. The file is a pure timetable, with no prose beyond its heads.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070031-8:
Decisions on AQUATONE are pressed in a memo dated 25 September 1956. The memo goes to the Acting Director after long thought on the project's future, its author states. It seeks full guidance from higher authority at the next meeting.

Uncertainty joined with inaction is hurting staff morale, the memo argues. Training of SAC crews for their own U-2 unit is about to start. Winter basing for three detachments needs a firm call if flights pause. If top targets stay barred for a time, flights against lesser areas are urged in set order. The craft's useful life has run down since its June exposure, the memo warns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100350003-8:
Buying under Project AQUATONE is reviewed in a memo dated 5 June 1958. The memo, copy 3 of 6 and marked SAPC, goes to the Director for information only. First phase contracts are now firm enough to judge, it states.

Buying has been joint in form from the start of the project. The Agency signs the contracts and funds the main items, the memo states. The Air Force supplies set government gear and buys items it can best develop. Lockheed Aircraft Corporation stands as prime contractor for the main work. The memo rests the joint form on section 10 of the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947. Contract SP-1913 is judged good for both sides in its close terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300060021-8:
Joint Jackson and Idealist flights are planned in a Secret paper on shared use of the U-2 force. Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Indonesia are named as areas of joint interest. Two deployment shapes are worked through in full detail.

One shape sends one aircraft and two pilots for a single mission, then pulls out fast. The other sends two aircraft and four pilots for ten missions in thirty days. Speed of the move guards security and keeps pilot fatigue down, the paper argues. Flights over denied ground hold near 70,000 feet, rising higher inside. In-flight refuelling trials at Detachment G have passed, with pilot training to follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300060030-8: An untitled declassified CIA document from the U-2 program collection. This CREST page sits among the IDEALIST files with no heading to guide the reader. A stray leaf from the spy plane archive, nameless but kept. The archive kept the page; only its heading slipped away with time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300240058-8:
Phase out of the IDEALIST program is broken to Kelly Johnson in a cable dated 28 June 1974. Wendell Bevan writes that the time has come to bare souls on the plan. Word should come from the source, not the rumor mill, he states.

Detachment H closes down from 25 July 1974, the cable states. Its two aircraft go back to SAC near 1 August 1974. Staff and gear pull out over 90 days, with doors locked near 1 November. Formal notice at the site waits until about 23 July by joint agreement. The Edwards detachment's Mid East work then passes to the Air Force 100th Wing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060011-8:
Annex of paragraph by paragraph notes explains the intent behind each numbered part of the agreement between the National Reconnaissance Office and the Joint Chiefs' Joint Reconnaissance Center. The first note states the aim of bringing older arrangements up to date. A 24 September 1958 agreement between the Air Force and Mr Dulles covered only the U-2. It also named men since replaced. A May 1963 defence memorandum is cited as agreeing the new setup in principle.

Resource notes give concrete cases: B-47 aircraft for peripheral work, Air Force U-2 flights over Cuba, and the 147 and AQ-12 drones among systems in development. Support given to CIA U-2 and A-12 missions is covered, while control of those missions stays with CIA. Later notes walk through transfer of control in tension, mission reporting, and keeping the Joint Chiefs informed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060048-8:
Agreement dated 13 March 1963 between the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence governs management of the National Reconnaissance Program. Its first article makes the Secretary of Defense the Executive Agent for the program, acting under policies agreed jointly with the Director. The aim stated is full use of the talents and resources found in both the Defense Department and the Agency.

To carry that charge, the Secretary sets up the National Reconnaissance Office as a separate operating agency of the Defense Department, under his direction and control. Its Director comes from the Defense side, named with the Director of Central Intelligence concurring, and gives most of his time to the Office. Its Deputy Director comes from CIA, named the same way in reverse, keeping the balance between the two houses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400070001-8:
Copy of the defence and CIA agreement on management of the National Reconnaissance Program survives in a scan rougher than most.
