It gives the Deputy Director of the NRO a defined place in the chain of command. He sits directly under the Director and must be kept fully and currently informed on all program activity at all times. Under the Director's hand he supervises ties with the United States Intelligence Board and its committees.

He also supervises all program tasks the Director assigns to CIA, and acts with the Director's full powers during absence or disability. Staff from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and CIA fill NRO posts full time. The chain of command runs from the Secretary of Defense, as Executive Agent, straight to the Director, and a functions section opens with work on a single national program of collection projects.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400130004-8:
Memorandum for the record dated 25 August 1961 sets down basic understandings between CIA and the Department of the Air Force on procurement under Project OXCART and KEDLOCK contracts. It builds on January 1956 letters between Trevor Gardner and Allen Dulles, a February 1956 record on AQUATONE buying, and the February 1960 OXCART organisation agreement signed by Dulles and General White.

The understandings renew a proven channel: CIA's special contract methods buy supplies and services the Air Force needs, in ways both sides found gainful under AQUATONE. CIA negotiates each contract from written Air Force requirements, and the Air Force side confirms each deal fits those requirements in full. Policy and procedure on such contracts follow the practice already in force on CIA's own OXCART procurements of the same kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400320003-8:
Memorandum dated 1 April 1967, sent to the Director of the National Reconnaissance Office, adds the case for moving the IDEALIST project to Davis Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona. It supplements a study of 14 March 1967 that listed reasons the move was not feasible. The memo instead lists advantages that might follow, on the same assumptions and with building costs at the new base accepted.

Chief gain named is closure of North Base at Edwards Air Force Base, possible once U-2R testing is largely done in about two years. The writer is candid that savings would be small: runway upkeep and fire protection are the main items, and support costs would rise at Davis Monthan as they fell at Edwards. Shared maintenance for the two U-2 fleets is raised, though sensor control must stay separate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400350028-8:
Memorandum for the record dated 13 April 1958 reports a personal equipment staff visit to Edwards and Del Rio Air Force Bases. Pilot morale is found good, and trust in the personal equipment staff acceptable. One sore point stood out: pilots assumed the project had let their gear slide, and that SAC pilots at Del Rio held far better kit.

A check at Del Rio showed the gear there was not superior, and the sore points were talked through with the pilots. Facility work to rebuild the pre-breathing, maintenance, and storage areas began on 31 March 1958. A long section covers ejection seats: all project aircraft are to get hot seats, at a weight penalty of fifty-three pounds, with hot and cold seats kept interchangeable in each aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400350118-8:
Letter dated 1 September 1955, on Air Force Office of Scientific Research letterhead from Baltimore, writes to the project's Deputy Director about aeromedical support. The writer sums up points settled in informal talks over the past month, and offers his reading of the agreements for correction if any item seems off. Medical responsibility is the first item taken up.

A project surgeon is to be assigned to the unit, working solely for it, with policy guidance flowing only through the Surgeon General, Major General Dan Ogle. The writer will brief the surgeon on past aeromedical work and on staffing needs. He presses hard on delays in getting medical airmen requested months before, fearing a crisis at first screening. A meeting on the scope of the professional support contract linked to Dr Lovelace is also being arranged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500060001-8:
Memorandum for General Ross forwards comments on U-2R carrier operations drawn from watching BLUE GULL V aboard USS America in November 1969. The verdict is favourable: the operation was well executed. The first landings were made in weather short of the best. The writer takes that as proof that flying the aircraft from a carrier deck is feasible. No problem arose that the crew could not handle.

Safety notes follow. Pilots should be trained to close the speed brakes on arrestment, since deck hands working near the hook stand inside their arc. The Navy norm of two landing signal officers, not the one used here, is urged for training and for spotting bad trends early. A pre-deployment briefing by ship's company, squeezed out this time, should be restored, and a named contact should man the ready room.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390104-8:
Memorandum GUS-0110, dated 29 January 1959, passes reconnaissance design guidelines for GUSTO to the Deputy Director for Plans. Two starting points shape the guidance: approval for long range penetration flights will stay hard to obtain, and each such flight must bring back the most information possible.

Only passive equipment should be used, the memo argues, ruling out radar sets that could reveal the aircraft. Two design paths follow, mixing visual photography with other sensors, or relying on sensors alone for poor weather and night work. Camera options for clear and adverse conditions are compared. The memo closes by urging early talks between camera designers and vehicle builders.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040039-8:
Weekend and holiday cover at Detachment H is defined in SOP H-20-3, dated 21 June 1968. The Staff Duty Officer is the point for choices and actions on off-duty days. He keeps the unit able to react while most staff are away. The Director of Support puts out the duty roster well ahead of time, where that can be done.

Duty officers may swap tours if Support hears of the change by noon on the last work day. The officer on duty must stay on base and tell section heads where he can be found. Choices on policy or flying go up to the commander or the operations chief first. A log form for each tour is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070018-8:
Keeping test project records, and clearing them out at the end, is governed by standing operating procedure 50-3055-20, dated 14 December 1964. Records means all papers created or picked up in support of a named test project. Each project has its own file, run by a Project Test Director, with a records officer watching the system as a whole for the organization.

Three rules open the policy: project papers must be complete, significant facts must be findable at any time, and files must be kept in a set order. Folder sections cover authority and program papers, test plans and procedures, travel support, test data, upkeep data, and system faults. Cover formats and contents lists are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050037-8:
Development Projects Division directive 10-2, dated 5 June 1962, tightens access to the DPD controlled area in the headquarters building. A letter K on a building badge had allowed free entry at all hours, and requests for it were rising fast. Action was taken to cut the number of non-DPD staff holding that free access to the 6B Wing restricted area.

Three groups are set instead. K is kept for DPD staff and others with a clear need for free entry. A second group goes on an access list and receives a temporary non-escort badge from the receptionist, with visits logged. Others enter as occasional visitors. Later papers cover contractor visits and care with classified material left out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020002-8:
Quarterly progress packet sent 16 January 1969 by Donald H. Ross covers OXCART and IDEALIST from 1 October to 31 December 1968. Tab A is a phase-out summary: OXCART property records were handled during a December period named in the text, as the closed program's affairs were settled. The packet carries five copies of each report for the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs.

IDEALIST work includes an engine pressure ratio schedule drawn from Pratt and Whitney study of flight test data. The schedule in use was judged too cautious, and a new one was being built from Detachment G data, to be checked at Detachment H for stall-free running in cold air. Film and filter tests for the wider intelligence community are also reported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800030001-8:
Memorandum 9258-72, dated 13 October 1972, forwards the IDEALIST progress report for 1 July to 30 September 1972. Wendell L. Bevan Jr. signs as Director of Special Activities. Three copies go to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. The report's development section leads with flight testing and qualification work under way during the summer quarter.

One delay is spelled out. The first modified B-3 camera with a new lens will arrive late in the second quarter. Its lens aspheric surface needs rework to fix a misalignment of its axis. Life support items include a new survival weapon folded into the seat kit, taking far less space than the old one. The semiannual life support conference, held in Washington on 2 August 1972, is also reported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800100003-8:
Status slides for IDEALIST, covering 1 April to 30 June 1971, list test flying at Detachment G, Edwards Air Force Base. Red Dot film tests used varied camera fits in the U-2C and U-2R, over eleven sorties. Other work included one hurricane photography sortie over Gulf Coast areas for the Office of Emergency Preparedness. Three sorties qualified a light weight monitor system. Two thermal tests of the Q bay were also flown.

A second slide set covers Detachment H for the same quarter. It reports fourteen missions alerted and eight flown. A note states that flown missions stayed at least twenty nautical miles off the coast of China. That limit matched an overflight suspension set by the 40 Committee, as the slide records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250007-8:
Memorandum 8914-68, dated 5 July 1968, gives the OXCART operational summary for 1 April to 30 June 1968. One A-12 overflight was flown in the period, launching from and returning to Kadena Air Base, Okinawa. The mission made two passes over targets in North Korea, with a flight time of 4 hours 6 minutes, as printed in the summary.

Fifteen SAM sites were covered: three occupied, one unoccupied, and eleven for identification only. Photo quality over the southern two-fifths of North Korea was fair to poor, with haze and cloud over about half the take. The summary notes this was the final BLACK SHIELD operational mission. Later pages cover redeployment from Kadena and nine A-12 aircraft placed in storage at Palmdale.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250016-8:
Progress packet 2691-67, signed by Paul N. Bacalis, forwards OXCART and IDEALIST reports for 1 July to 30 September 1967. Five copies of each go to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. Status tables place A-12 aircraft and pilots at Kadena Air Base, Okinawa, and note that aircraft 122 entered flyable storage at Palmdale on 16 September 1967, as the attachment records.

The IDEALIST section marks a milestone: the first flight of the U-2R took place at Edwards Air Force Base, California, on 25 August 1967, with more flights since. A visit to Pratt and Whitney follows in the propulsion section. Closing research notes cover a proposal to cut induced drag on high altitude aircraft, forwarded to the Director, National Reconnaissance Office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100090006-8:
Administrative Service, Office of the Chief, presents a statement of functions with a table of organization and position status headings. The chief's office holds overall coordination, supervision, policy, procedures, and general management of the service's divisions. It also runs liaison with CIA activities and other bodies named in the text, as the statement records.

Because the service's work is spread across many buildings, the chief and his two deputies follow a visiting schedule. Each of them visits two divisions per week, to talk through current and coming programs and problems. The file repeats the statement and contents pages across several scanned pages, with the same headings carried through each copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030119-8:
CIA procedure regulation on building maintenance and utilities, departmental area, tells offices how to ask for alterations and installations in agency buildings. Requests go to the Chief, Administrative Services, on Form No. 36-7 or by memorandum in duplicate. They should state the service needed and its justification in specific terms, with drawings or sketches where practical, and name a contact person for the work.

The Building Maintenance and Utilities Division supplies engineers when needed and helps plan projects. Work touching the physical security of an area is sent for recommendation or approval before action. Further sections cover real estate and construction beyond the departmental area, with requests routed to the Real Estate and Construction Division. A reproduction section at the end repeats the rule that signed requests go to the Reproduction Division chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030128-8:
CIA regulation on reproduction requires each office head to name staff, at GS-7 or above, who may authorize reproduction services for that office. Names go in writing to the Chief, Administrative Services, and changes must also be reported in writing. The point is control of demand on the agency's reproduction plant, which the regulation calls heavy.

Authorized staff must learn the services on offer, the time each takes, and its cost, so the cheapest suitable process is chosen and copy counts kept low. All signed requests go to the chief of the Reproduction Division. Equipment requests route through that chief as well. Later sections in the file cover telephone and teletype requests, cafeteria liaison, and hot plate installation, which requires a fireproof base and a checked power circuit before use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050036-8:
Federal Register issue for Friday, 22 December 1950, volume 15, number 248, is bound into this file as printed pages. Its lead item under Title 3, The President, is Executive Order 10195. That order names Korea and adjacent waters a combat zone for income tax purposes. It acts under section 22(b)(13) of the Internal Revenue Code, as amended by the Revenue Act of 1950.

The zone is drawn by coordinates. It runs from latitude 39 degrees 30 minutes north down the 122 degrees 45 minutes east line. It then crosses to 133 degrees east, and up to the coast where Korea meets the USSR. Later pages carry other register matter. Transportation allowance rules set net weight at eighty percent of packed weight. Agriculture conservation payment rates for pipe by diameter also appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050144-8:
Memorandum for the Chief, Services Branch, marked as reviewed by the Office of General Counsel on 25 November 1947, returns a redraft of proposed delegations of authority with suggested changes underlined. Wording points lead: the title Director of Central Intelligence is restored, matching the original delegation, and one word is swapped because the first suggested text above it in the same paper. A specific rescission clause is added, and renumbering is proposed.

The delegation text follows. Its root is a Director's memorandum of 24 July 1947. The Chief or Assistant Chief, Supply Division, may sign unnumbered contracts where payment is a single remittance under 2,000 dollars. The draft stresses that no exception to the single payment rule exists for this agency, so contracting officers, contractors, and the General Accounting Office are all on notice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050171-8:
Agreement dated 27 November 1946 moves the State Department printing plant at 2430 E Street, Northwest, to the Government Printing Office. The three parties are the Department of State, the Central Intelligence Group, and the Government Printing Office. The plant is transferred and will be operated by the printing office under 44 U.S.C. 60, subject to the agreement's terms.

A list of plant staff and equipment to move will go to a policy committee for concurrence. Extra equipment and staff needed for sound running will be supplied by the printing office. In running the plant, the printing office will follow the security rules of State or the Central Intelligence Group, whichever is higher for the work in hand. Payment for work is under section 601 of the Economy Act. The transfer takes effect on or before 1 March 1947.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050199-8:
Annotated edition of the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, issued by the General Services Administration under Administrator Jess Larson, pairs the act's text with analysis and a full index. The act's contents run from organization of the new administration through property management: buying and warehousing, use of excess property, surplus disposal, proceeds, and surveys, standardization, and cataloging.

The analysis explains section by section why provisions read as they do. One note on uncollectible claims stresses the wide discretion staff need when vast amounts of property must be moved swiftly. Civil penalties for fraud are analyzed, with three measures of damages open to the United States. The index closes the volume, running from personnel holding appointments under the Surplus Property Act of 1944 to warehousing and woolen goods disposal, with section numbers for each entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200070043-8:
Draft procedures dated January 1949, written under a memorandum of 29 December 1948 from the Executive Director, govern handling of signal property by the Services Office and the Communications Division, OSO. Accountability records will be kept in the Storage and Issue Section of the Supply Division. The Communications Division will keep its own memorandum record of stock on hand, posted from requisitions. Copies of all vouchers posted by the accountable officer will be sent to it for information.

Nomenclature comes next. The two offices will review all signal equipment on hand and fix complete, accurate names for every item, with a stock numbering system agreed between them. Receiving is a Services Office duty; technical inspection belongs to the Inspection and Testing Section. Shipments are coordinated with the Transportation Section, and cancellations must be reported by memorandum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100003-8:
Monthly report of operations for the period ending 31 August 1953, from the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch. Personnel figures show eighteen Mail Control staff on leave of three days or more, ten in Records Management, and three at the Records Center. One man is detailed full time as a courier to the Transportation Division. New applicants interviewed and recruiting by office and by Personnel are also tabled.

Administration notes lead with meetings with two groups of area records officers. Points at issue between the branch and the offices are mostly settled, the report states, and the assignment should finish within the next month. Project 5-53, rewriting the CIA Correspondence Manual, has been revised after agency comments and will circulate through area records officers. Filming for the month totals 23,978 images: 3,780 by rotary camera and 20,198 by flatbed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100020027-8:
Office memorandum dated 25 January 1949, headed random notes on the TRS reorganization, argues staffing points for the Office of Deputy for Special Projects. An administrative officer is needed on that staff at least half time. One named staff member now spends about seventy-five percent of her time on such problems, the notes say. She has become the person everyone turns to when anything needs doing, and an unmatched source on training problems across Buildings 13 and 14.

A clerk-stenographer is called urgent, in line with a memo of 12 January 1949. Tests and measurements staffing is also pressed: an instructor with a degree in educational psychology, strong on test construction, is wanted. The writer notes he gives two to four hours a day to OPC interests, with no OPC officer provided on the staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020041-8:
Results of a conference of 22 July 1952 record agreements between the head of IT/D and the Plans and Policy Staff. The subject is the Career Service Committee report's effect on the Basic Intelligence Course. The conference worked from P&P notes. All statements of the situation in them were accepted. On the program's objective, doubt should clear once a definition of professional enters a CIA regulation. The 14 July draft was accepted.

On specialized skills, TR(G) will wait and see. The head of IT/D leans more on on-the-job training than P&P. Student numbers beyond the capacity of Alcott Wing B are to be planned for. Staff totals are nine CIA staff, four from other agencies, and a training assistant. Space ratios close the paper: one classroom for each twenty-five to thirty students, and no more than two instructors to an office.

National Security Council directive, issued under section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947 as amended, sets the rules that govern United States work in this field. dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-8:
For books sixty-one through seventy, the full text of Dio Cassius is lost. His history comes down in the shortened form made by Xiphilinus, a Byzantine monk. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation prints that epitome in this eighth volume. The years run from Nero to the reign of Trajan.

Nero's fall, the year of four emperors, and the Flavian house pass in quick, sharp scenes. The Jewish war and the reigns of Titus and Domitian follow, then Nerva and the start of Trajan. Even cut down, Dio stays a main source for the first century of emperors. The volume shows how much a good epitome can save.
doe-osti-17120794-analysis-of-the-1-404-: Krypton-84's 1.404 keV resonance got analyzed, and this DOE report covers the neutron capture resonance. The pages detail the measurement. The nuclear data folks get their numbers. The resonance was 1.404 keV. The numbers were nuclear. The capture was neutron. The isotope was krypton-84.
doe-osti-2997987-fy24-fy25-efforts-to-re: Liquid metal fire protection got revived, and this DOE effort covers the ANS-54.8 standard. The pages detail the FY24-25 work. The reactor safety folks get their update. The standard was ANS-54.8. The plants were LMR. The folks were reactor safety.
froude-history-england-vol-8:
Elizabeth's middle years steady England in the eighth volume of Froude's History, from 1856. The Protestant settlement takes firmer root across the realm. Drake and the sea dogs rise to fame on daring voyages and raids against Spain.

Froude writes the fifteen seventies and eighties with stirring pace. England finds its footing as a sea power and a Protestant state. Courtiers, sailors, and settlers all advance his broad national tale. The volume bridges the plot-haunted early reign and the Armada crisis ahead, showing a kingdom growing in wealth, confidence, and reach under its watchful queen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-8:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes for the afternoon of July 17, 1945, record debate on Britain's part in the Japan war. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Sir Alan Brooke led for the British Chiefs of Staff.

The chiefs first approved the conclusions of their 193rd meeting. Brooke then took up the British contribution papers, numbers 889 and 889/1. He said his chiefs were very pleased with the U.S. answer. The U.S. Chiefs agreed in principle to a British Commonwealth land force in the war's final phase. That agreement hung on settling operational problems with the U.S. Pacific commanders. It also hung on clarifying certain factors, which Brooke then proposed to deal with point by point.
gao-gaoreports-b-294358-8:
University Research Company returns in companion files B-294358.8 through B-294358.10, dated April 6, 2006. The same Health Information Network contract was at stake, after a court-ordered review of reproduction costs. GAO denied the protest. The agency had fairly kept its earlier scores when the fix was limited to revised offers on reproduction services alone. That approach matched the evaluation scheme in the solicitation.

A second point defends an upward adjustment to the protester's own stated costs. The change fit a quirk in its cost offer. Without it, the cost scoring would have lost its power to predict real prices.
gao-gaoreports-b-309752-8:
A plea to rethink a logistics ruling is refused in this GAO decision, B-309752.8, dated December 20, 2007. Kellogg, Brown & Root Services, Inc. sought a fresh look at an October ruling. That ruling upheld protests of Army logistics awards. The deal backs combat troops with global support work. It is known by the short name LOGCAP.

The firm claimed four flaws in the first ruling. It said harm to fair play was not shown. It said GAO used facts outside the score file. It said an audit report was misread. It said talks should not reopen. GAO denied the plea on each point. The first ruling stands as issued.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-8:
Bank rule-making by a federal regulator is examined in GAO-06-8, a report GAO released on October 17, 2005. On January 13, 2004, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued two sets of preemption rules. The rules set how far the National Bank Act overrides state and local laws for national banks. State officials protested both the rules and the way they were written. GAO reviewed the consultation and documentation behind the process.

GAO found that the office generally followed the requirements for rule-making. But it lacked documentation and written guidance for its consultation steps. That gap made its outreach efforts hard to verify. The office did consider all comments on one rule and changed parts in response. GAO saw chances to strengthen both consultation and record keeping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-8:
Reviews of disability benefits are examined in GAO-07-8, dated October 3, 2006. The Social Security Administration must find medical improvement before it can end benefits. That rule guards people on Disability Insurance and Supplemental Security Income. Each year, about 13,800 beneficiaries leave the rolls under this standard. GAO surveyed all 55 state disability determination offices. It asked how often people improve and what makes the standard hard to apply.

Examiners told GAO the rules leave key points unclear. Seven of 11 examiners were unsure when to use exceptions to the standard. Doubt also clouds how much improvement counts as enough. Views on the presumption of continued disability vary as well. Those gaps can make like cases end in unlike ways. GAO urged the agency to clarify its guidance on each point. The agency saw value in more guidance. It doubted the need for more on the exceptions, though.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-8:
Saving for old age now rests mostly on workers themselves. Pay-in plans tied to each worker's own account have replaced most set-benefit pensions over 25 years. GAO-08-8, dated November 29, 2007, measures how much workers hold in such plans and what they may hold at retirement.

Only 36 percent of workers took part in a current plan in 2004 data. The median balance was $22,800, and $60,600 for workers aged 60 to 64. Forecasts for workers born in 1990 show about 37 percent reaching retirement with no plan savings at all. Low-income workers fare worst. The report weighs ideas to widen coverage.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-8:
A doctor discovers poison in his town's baths and gets branded an enemy for telling the truth. An Enemy of the People shares Archer's eighth volume, from 1908, with The Wild Duck, Ibsen's tragicomic study of self-deception. The pairing shows the playwright's two faces in one binding.

Doctor Stockmann rages against the compact majority that prefers profit to honesty. The Wild Duck turns inward, asking whether stripping away comforting lies always heals or sometimes kills. Idealism's fire and the poet's pity stand side by side. Critics rank both plays among the most perfectly built in all drama. English readers meet them in the classic Archer versions.
lecky-england-18th-vol-8:
Georgian England transforms in the eighth and final volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. Steam and factories remake the land and its towns at speed. A religious revival stirs the nation's soul while reformers press the first claims for a wider vote.

Eight volumes end with a country changed beyond all recognition. The old world of farms and coaches gives way to mills and railways. Lecky closes at the threshold of modern Britain with calm survey. His great history stands complete at last. It is vast, fair, and humane: a portrait of a century that made the modern world.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-8:
Part Eight opens with the Professor's Yarn in Chapter 36. The narrator was once a humble young land-surveyor, he says. A California mining-ditch survey sent him on a sea voyage. Three or four weeks aboard ship lay ahead of him.

Three professional gamblers played daily in an upper-deck stateroom. Their door stood ajar, leaking tobacco smoke and profanity. A countrified, good-natured passenger kept seeking his company. Reading and dreaming were the surveyor's passions, conversation was not. Tobacco smoke and profanity escaped through the gamblers' ajar door. The countrified passenger's beaming good nature engaged him despite himself.
nasa-tm-19710010481-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 8 of the Manned Spacecraft Center's Apollo 13 Investigation Team surveyed high-pressure oxygen systems after the April 1970 explosion. This addendum to its final report, dated March 1971, reviews how materials were judged safe for use with liquid or gaseous oxygen. The panel asked whether existing test methods really captured the ways materials catch fire in oxygen.

The introduction explains that qualification had rested on past use or on impact and friction tests, the most common ignition sources. The panel lists other triggers, including sparks, electrical shorts, shocks, and bulk heating, and notes that powered systems break the old assumptions. It also stresses what happens after ignition: whether a material quenches itself, burns slowly, burns fast, or explodes. The report then assesses current liquid and gaseous oxygen test methods and their competence for spacecraft use.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-8:
Volume eight of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, is given to Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms. The volume came out in 1886 under Philip Schaff. Augustine preached and dictated on all 150 psalms across some thirty years of his bishopric.

His method is allegory: every verse of the psalm is heard as the voice of Christ and his church. A psalm's cry of pain becomes the church suffering; its praise, the church rejoicing. The work is vast, uneven, and beloved. Medieval preachers mined it endlessly, and it shaped how the West prayed the psalter. The volume closes the Augustine block of Schaff's first series.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-8:
Basil the Great's letters and select works fill volume eight of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Basil, bishop of Caesarea, organized eastern monastic life and fought for the Nicene faith. His letters alone run to more than three hundred. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

The letters show Basil at work: settling quarrels, begging tax relief for the poor, and coaching young monks. His treatise on the Holy Spirit argues the Spirit's full divinity from the church's worship. His nine homilies on the six days of creation mix scripture with sharp eyes for nature. The volume is the record of a bishop who built hospitals and a theology at once.
peter-s-pence-sailor-s-knots-part-8:
"Peter's Pence" comes from W. W. Jacobs's Sailor's Knots of 1909, and the night-watchman tells it. Sailors, he says, don't bother much about relations, partly because relations expect presents. Peter Russet has just come home after ten months away, money in pocket, with Sam Small and Ginger Dick beside him.

A letter waiting at the office ruins the planned spree. Peter's old uncle George Goodman, unseen for twenty years, is in London for the first time in thirty-three and wants to stay with Peter and be shown about. Jacobs builds the comedy from Peter's dread and his mates' curiosity.
podcast-joerogan-9uhx6ApHD-8:

roughing-it-part-8:
Part 8 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter LXXI. The party winds down a hill of old lava to the sea at four in the afternoon. Flow after flow of fire, Twain says, built the island higher over long ages. The rock below is honey-combed with caves, so wells will not hold water and planters rely on rain tanks. In one place lava closed round a grove of cocoa-nut trees, leaving holes that keep the print of bark, knots, branches, leaves, and nuts.

Soon the party sees Kealakekua Bay, where Captain Cook was killed by the islanders nearly a hundred years before. A summer shower falls as the setting sun flames on the bay, and two bright rainbows span it. Two men riding ahead pass through one bow, and for a moment their clothes shine with more than royal splendor.

the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-8:
Part eight of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter thirty-two, late on a Tuesday, with the village of St. Petersburg still in mourning. The lost children have not been found, and the search has worn out hope.

Public prayers have been offered, and many a private prayer with a whole heart in it, yet no good news comes from the cave. Most searchers have gone back to their daily work, sure the children are lost for good. Mrs. Thatcher lies very ill, calling for her child in her raving, while Aunt Polly's gray hair has gone near white. Then, in the middle of the night, the village bells burst out in a wild peal.
the-changing-numbers-odd-craft-part-8:
W. W. Jacobs placed this short tale in his Odd Craft gathering, under the title The Changing Numbers. The scene is a small living room at eight in the evening, where a tall clock stands in the corner. Mr. Samuel Gunnill comes down the winding stairs with great care and humility.

His daughter Selina seems lost in tending the plants at the window, and no sign of breakfast preparations appears. She snips dead leaves with exact care, waters like a druggist mixing a dose, then sighs with a force no plant could explain. A second sigh draws a meek cough from her father. She turns fast, upright, with surprise and anger mixed in her look, and the talk begins over a white plant at the row's end. Jacobs builds the comedy from such small household signals.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-8:
Volume eight of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with Jesus and the woman taken in adultery. John's text tells how the scribes and Pharisees set her before him as a trap. Jesus writes on the ground, then says the sinless one should cast the first stone. Her accusers slip away one by one, eldest first, and he sends her off forgiven.

Next comes the raising of Lazarus, called from the tomb after four days. Doré's plates give both scenes grave weight. Mercy and power over death stand side by side in this volume.
the-poetical-works-of-william-wordsworth: Volume II of The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, edited by William Knight and dated 1896, is the second of eight volumes. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents open with Peter Bell. Lines composed above Tintern Abbey follow, written on revisiting the Wye on July 13, 1798. Pieces from 1799 come next, among them There was a Boy, Nutting, and The Simplon Pass. The Lucy poems appear too, beginning Strange fits of passion and She dwelt among the untrodden ways.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-8:
Part 8 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XXVII, In Prison. The cells are crowded, so Hendon and the King are chained in a large room with some twenty prisoners of both sexes and all ages, a foul-mouthed, noisy crowd. The King chafes at the indignity to his royalty. Hendon is bewildered instead. He had come home a jubilant prodigal and got the cold shoulder and a jail.

His thoughts settle on Edith, whose conduct he turns over in all lights. Did she know him, or did she not? He ends convinced that she did know him and repudiated him for interested reasons. Yet her name has been sacred too long for him to curse it. The night passes in soiled prison blankets, amid liquor, ribald songs, and fighting. A jailer's clubbing restores peace after a prisoner nearly kills a woman with his manacles.
the-temptation-of-samuel-burge-captains-:
W. W. Jacobs opens The Temptation of Samuel Burge, a story from his Captains All collection, in the small parlour behind Mr. Higgs's jewellery shop. A supper table stands laid and untouched at a quarter to ten. Higgs rubs his hands over the fire, hungry, and wonders what etiquette says about starting before the expected guest arrives. His housekeeper blames London gentlemen and their late hours.

The guest is Brother Burge, a celebrated chapel preacher from Clerkenwell who supposedly lives only for the work. Talk turns to Brother Simpson, who called kitchen smells the flesh-pots of Egypt. Higgs admits he fancies Burge was a little wild in his younger days. Jacobs sets a comic trap: a saintly visitor, a waiting supper, and hosts already doubting the saint.
the-vigil-night-watches-part-8:
W. W. Jacobs stages The Vigil as a courtship under threat in the eighth of his Night Watches pieces. Mr. Farrer declares himself the happiest man in the world, and Miss Ward sighs that he should wait until her father comes in. The father is ex-Sergeant-Major Ward, whose firm, springy step the young man dreads hearing outside.

Miss Ward's mother favours the match but hides in her bedroom, hating unpleasantness. The sergeant-major wants a soldier for a son-in-law and thinks modern young men too soft. When the lamp is lit with the blind still up, the old warrior bursts in on an embrace and roars his questions. Jacobs times the discovery like a stage farce.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-8:
Volume 8 closes Thirlwall's History of Greece, in a text dated 1832. Alexander and the Hellenistic world he made fill the final book. Greece, beaten at home, spreads its culture across the East.

Cities, language, and learning travel from Egypt to India in Alexander's wake. Thirlwall ends his eight volumes on that wide, mixed legacy. Greek arms lose an empire while Greek thought wins a world. His liberal history finds a fitting, thoughtful close in this paradox. Readers leave with a full arc from myth to world empire. Few English histories of Greece from his age match its span.
un-ga-res-8:
Millions of people had no home to go back to when the Second World War ended. Resolution 8 of the General Assembly, passed on 12 February 1946, calls the plight of refugees and displaced people a matter of instant urgency. It also draws a sharp line: true refugees must not be confused with war criminals, quislings, and traitors, who could claim no such shelter.

The whole question is sent to the Economic and Social Council for a full study, with a report due at the next part of the session. A special team should be formed to do the work fast. The text lays down tests for the study, among them that the plight is world-wide in scope.
un-ga-res-a-69-8: Joint work with a bloc of central European states fills Resolution A/69/8, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Central European Initiative had held observer status at the Assembly since 2011. The text praises the bloc's work to deepen its ties with the UN family and with other world and regional bodies. Its aim is a real, good mark on the politics and wealth of the region, through shared projects in its chief fields.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 8 (I) of the General Assembly was adopted on 12 February 1946. It sets the first United Nations policy for the millions of refugees and displaced persons left by the Second World War. The Assembly sends the question to the Economic and Social Council for full examination, including the work of the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees.

The resolution lays down guiding principles. The main task for refugees and displaced persons is early return home. No refugee with valid objections may be compelled to go back to his country of origin. The problem must not be confused with the surrender and punishment of war criminals, quislings, and traitors. Those who left because of Nazi or fascist persecution fall outside the suspicion cast on collaborators. So do those who fought on the democratic side. These principles framed how the new organization approached the postwar refugee crisis.

Resolution 69/8, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, covers cooperation between the United Nations and the Central European Initiative. The Initiative marked its twenty-fifth anniversary that November. It welcomes the Initiative's 2014-2016 plan of action. The plan covers transport, energy, the environment, small businesses and research. It notes its project funds and cooperation with the European Union. It invites closer dialogue between the two secretariats.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Nine hopeful states applied to the young UN, and three got in by this vote of 1946. The Council adopted Resolution 8 at its 57th meeting. Ten members voted yes and none voted no. Australia held back. The bids came from Albania, Mongolia, and Afghanistan. Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal applied as well. Iceland, Siam, and Sweden rounded out the nine.

The Council weighed each bid in debate, the text says. It then urges the Assembly to admit just three states. Afghanistan, Iceland, and Sweden make the cut. The rest fell to early Cold War feuds. The split foretold the admissions freeze of the next decade. A package deal broke that freeze in 1955.
vittoria-volume-8: The last of eight volumes of George Meredith's Vittoria stands as number 48 in the Gutenberg series of his works. Pages present here give the old Project Gutenberg header and nothing else, so the closing chapters of the novel do not appear. The header closes with word of the Literary Archive Foundation, a nonprofit body that holds the files. With this volume the split set ends; a companion record preserves the full contents of the whole novel in one list.
